title: Falsy traps
prompt_md: Truthiness is convenient until a legitimate value happens to be falsy. Work through these, paying attention to which values are falsy and what `and`/`or` actually return.

questions.stem_md: A handler contains `limit = limit or 100`. A caller passes `limit=0`, meaning "return nothing". What happens?
questions.explanation_md: `0` is falsy, so `or` moves on and evaluates its right operand. The pattern means "if the value is falsy, replace it", not "if the value is missing, replace it". Use `limit = 100 if limit is None else limit`.

questions.stem_md: Which of these are **falsy** in Python?
questions.explanation_md: Zero of any numeric type and every empty built-in container are falsy. A non-empty string is truthy regardless of what it contains: `"0"` and `" "` are both truthy, which is why validating user input with `if value:` accepts `"0"` and rejects `""`. Midnight was falsy in Python 2 but is truthy from 3.5 onwards.

questions.stem_md: Complete both defaults so that `0`, `[]` and `""` survive as real arguments.
questions.explanation_md: `is None` is an identity test, so it is true only for `None` itself: `0`, `[]` and `""` all pass through untouched. When `None` is a legitimate value, a module-level `object()` instance works as a unique sentinel: nothing a caller can construct is identical to it.

sources.locator: Comparisons to singletons like None should use is or is not

questions.stem_md: What does the expression `[] or "fallback"` evaluate to? Give the exact value.
questions.explanation_md: `or` returns one of its operands, not a boolean. Since `[]` is falsy it returns the right operand, the string `"fallback"`. Symmetrically, `"a" and 0` returns `0`, and `[] and boom()` never calls `boom` at all: short-circuiting is why `if user and user.is_active` is safe.

questions.stem_md: A class defines both `__bool__` returning `False` and `__len__` returning `5`. What is `bool(instance)`?

options.md: `False`: `__bool__` is consulted first and `__len__` is never called.
Undefined; it depends on the interpreter.

questions.explanation_md: The protocol is: try `__bool__`, fall back to `__len__() != 0`, and default to true if neither exists. That fallback is why every empty container is falsy without defining `__bool__`, and why a custom class with no `__len__` is always truthy, including one that wraps an empty result set.

hints.md: Two facts unlock most of this: zero-of-any-type and every empty container are falsy, and `and`/`or` return one of their **operands** rather than `True`/`False`.

For the default-argument questions, ask what the caller could legitimately pass that happens to be falsy. `0`, `[]`, `""` and `False` are all real values someone may mean. Identity (`is`) tests for one specific object; truthiness tests for a whole class of values.

Answers: (1) `limit` becomes `100`: the caller's `0` is swallowed. (2) Falsy: `0.0`, `[]`, `Decimal("0")`, `{}`; truthy: `"0"`, `" "`, `time(0, 0)`. (3) `is`, then `object`. (4) `"fallback"`. (5) `False`: `__bool__` wins and `__len__` is never consulted.
